description: I’m forming a team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge focused on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator. I have experience in coding and I’m excited to use AI to build smart, practical solutions. I’m looking for collaborators who are curious, committed, and ready to work together to design a tool that helps plan safe and effective landing paths on the Moon
summary:
LUNA Mission Control is a web app for planning safe landings and spacewalks at the Moon's south pole, built on real NASA data.

The app shows a 3D Moon made from NASA's lunar elevation maps (LOLA) and nine candidate Artemis landing regions with more detailed local terrain. It uses NASA JPL Horizons to work out where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky for any date. From that it maps which places get sunlight, which can talk to Earth, and which are steep, then ranks landing sites with a go/no-go result. It also counts down to the next spacewalk window and forecasts 30 days ahead. A powered-descent simulator lands an Apollo-style lander under lunar gravity with limited fuel. The "AI analyse & land" button searches the terrain and tests possible approaches. An AI then explains the chosen plan, and a separate, tested autopilot flies the landing.

This matters because NASA's Artemis IV is aiming for the first crewed south-pole landing in 2028. At the pole, the Sun stays low, long shadows cover the ground, and contact with Earth can be lost. LUNA turns that real data into clear, interactive decisions for students, the public and mission planners, while stating its limits openly.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

LUNA Mission Control is a web app that helps plan safe landings and spacewalks at the Moon's south pole. It renders a full 3D Moon built from NASA's real LOLA elevation data, with nine historical Artemis candidate landing regions available as detailed 80-metre terrain grids. Using NASA JPL Horizons, it calculates where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky for any date, then maps sunlight, Earth communication contact, slope, and overall operability across the terrain. A planner ranks the five best landing sites, and an "AI analyse & land" feature searches the terrain for a verified safe target, explains each check it performs, gets an advisory AI assessment, and then flies an automatic landing in a realistic simulator with lunar gravity, finite fuel, and real terrain contact.

What benefits does it have?

It turns complex orbital and terrain data into clear, visual go/no-go decisions. Users can see why a site is safe or unsafe — sunlight hours, Earth contact windows, slope — rather than trusting a black box. The simulator lets anyone experience how hard a polar landing actually is.

What is the intended impact?

With Artemis IV targeting the first crewed south-pole landing in 2028, public understanding of the mission's challenges matters. LUNA makes real mission-planning science accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts, and demonstrates how AI can assist — without replacing — verified engineering calculations.

Tools, languages, and software used

TypeScript and React (TanStack Start), Three.js/React Three Fiber for 3D rendering, Web Workers for horizon ray-tracing, NASA LOLA LDEM elevation data, NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris, NASA LROC WAC imagery, an Apollo lunar module 3D model, Lovable Cloud for the AI gateway (GPT-based advisory assessments), and Vitest for testing. No special hardware — it runs in any browser.

How is it creative?

It combines real NASA terrain, live orbital mechanics, an explainable AI site-selection process, and a hands-on flight simulator in one interactive experience — most tools do only one of these. The AI narrates its reasoning stage by stage, so users learn the science while watching it work.

What factors did I consider?

Safety first: the AI is advisory only and can never control the engines — all flight decisions come from tested, deterministic physics. Accuracy: real NASA data with honestly stated limits (approximate region centres, 80 m grid spacing, no rock-level hazard data). Transparency: every data source is linked and dated. Accessibility: works on desktop and mobile with no installation.
dataRefs: NASA LOLA Global Elevation Map (LDEM_4_FLOAT) — whole-Moon terrain, 4 pixels per degree
NASA LOLA South Pole Elevation Map (LDEM_80S_80M) — detailed 80 m terrain for the south pole and the nine candidate regions
NASA Moon Trek — LROC WAC Global Mosaic — real lunar surface imagery mapped onto the terrain
NASA JPL Horizons Ephemeris System — real Sun and Earth positions in the lunar sky for any date
NASA Artemis III Candidate Landing Regions (2024 announcement and map) — the nine candidate regions shown in the app
NASA Apollo Lunar Module 3D Model — the lander used in the simulator (NASA public-domain model)
NASA Artemis Mission Updates — the mission timeline in the briefing (Artemis II–IV)
LROC QuickMap — linked as an external reference map
